#6663. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6662. How To Roast Butternut Squash

Roasting is my favorite way to prepare butternut squash, hands down. The high, fast heat of the oven brings out the squash’s natural sweetness and eliminates excess moisture, concentrating all that flavor into a smaller package. Once roasted, the squash is ready to be pureed into soups, tossed into grain bowls—or simply eaten by the forkful. While many roasted butternut squash recipes restrict seasonings to just salt and pepper, I’m going a little extra here. Yes, there is a basic recipe for simply seasoned squash if you want to puree it into soup or use it as the base for a creamy orzo skillet, but I’ve also given you a few other options to try if you want to give the squash more personality. The garlic-herb variation is just begging to be tossed into a salad as “squash croutons,” and the sweet ’n’ spicy is so good I almost ate it all, straight off the baking sheet.

For the basic roasted butternut squash recipe, preheat the oven to 425° with the rack in the middle position. Line a large baking sheet with foil to make for easier cleanup.

Spread the cubed squash out onto the foil-lined sheet, drizzle with olive oil, and sprinkle with salt, then use a flexible rubber spatula to toss the squash until everything is evenly incorporated. Spread the squash back out into an even layer, making sure the pieces are not crowding each other. (If they’re too close together, they’ll steam and you’ll lose some of that great caramelization.) Season the squash with freshly ground black pepper.

Roast the squash, undisturbed, until tender and lightly caramelized on the bottom, 25 to 30 minutes. Remove the baking sheet from the oven and let the squash cool slightly before removing.

For the sweet ’n’ spicy variation, preheat the oven to 425°, with the rack in the middle position. Line a large baking sheet with foil.

In a large bowl, toss together the squash and olive oil. (I know it might seem weird to use a bowl here when we’re just tossing on the baking sheet for the basic version, but this is because the spices tend to stick to the baking sheet and burn while the squash is roasting.) Sprinkle the garam masala, salt, sweet paprika, cumin, and cayenne over the squash, and toss everything until evenly coated. Finally, drizzle the spiced squash with the honey and toss to combine.

Spread the seasoned squash out on the foil-lined baking sheet, making sure the pieces don’t crowd each other too much. Roast, undisturbed, until tender and caramelized on the bottom, 25 to 30 minutes. (I recommend checking at the 20-minute mark to make sure the pieces of squash on the outside of the baking sheet are not caramelizing too fast on the bottom. If they are, just flip the pieces that are getting dark on the bottom.) Remove the baking sheet from the oven and let the squash cool slightly before removing.

For the garlic-herb variation, preheat the oven to 425°, with the rack in the middle position. Line a large baking sheet with foil.

Spread the cubed squash out onto the foil-lined sheet, drizzle with olive oil, and sprinkle with salt, then use a flexible rubber spatula to toss the squash until everything is evenly incorporated. Spread the squash back out into an even layer, making sure the pieces are not crowding each other.

Roast the squash, undisturbed, until it’s just beginning to be tender (about 20 minutes), then remove the baking sheet from the oven and sprinkle with the garlic, thyme, and sage, then return the baking sheet to the oven and roast until the garlic is golden and the squash is tender and lightly caramelized on the bottom, about 10 minutes more. Remove the baking sheet from the oven and let the squash cool slightly before removing.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Roasted butternut squash is wonderful fresh, but it also makes good meal prep! If you’d like to make it ahead of time, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days.

Nutrition (per serving): 135 calories, 2 g protein, 19 g carbohydrates, 6 g fiber, 4 g sugar, 7 g fat, 1 g saturated fat, 487 mg sodium

Bakeware and cookware courtesy of Crate & Barrel.

#6661. Zohran Mamdani’s Mustache Is Singlehandedly Bringing Movember Back

When New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani passed out water bottles to marathoners on Nov. 1, few clocked the newly mustachioned man as the city’s head honcho. After all, he’s the first bearded NYC mayor in over a century after, and his constituents had grown familiar with his signature look. When images of his new facial hair circulated, people wondered what inspired the change. Had the mayor been influenced by his hip Brooklyn constituents enough to grow his own on-trend mustache? As we learned the day after the marathon in an online video, the mustache was in support of a somewhat-ancient tradition: Movember.

If it feels like no one’s talked about Movember for a while, that’s because the non-profit charity’s heyday online peaked in 2012. That year, according to the Australian-based foundation, over 1.1 million people participated in Movember—a campaign that encourages men to grow mustaches to raise awareness and funds for men’s mental health, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer—collecting more than $126 million in charity. But like planking, “Gangnam Style,” and flash mobs, Movember eventually faded from the cultural conversation. Google Trends recorded a 10% drop in searches for the cause the following year, and by 2026, search interest had fallen 90% from its 2012 peak. Now, after Mamdani, alongside Council Member Rita Joseph, announced a $4 million investment in a new prostate cancer center at Brooklyn’s Kings County Hospital in honor of the hairy month-long social movement, interest in Movember has since climbed to its highest level since 2019, according to Google Trends.

While the mayor’s stubble has come and gone throughout the month, the heavy mustache has remained constant.

The stubble around the mustache has come and gone during the month, but that thick mustache has remained a staple. He had it at a Veterans Day reception, during a plethora of press conferences, and when he announced the disbanding of the New York Police Department’s controversial Strategic Response Group.

Politicians have long been defined, at least in part, by their hair: Donald Trump’s comb-over, Bernie Sanders’ horseshoe-shaped hairline, Gavin Newsom’s slicked-back locks. But facial hair is increasingly becoming part of the political image, too, as more men embrace letting their beards grow. Pete Buttigieg, once clean-shaven, grew a beard after leaving his post as Transportation Secretary; JD Vance became the first bearded vice president in decades; and Mamdani ended more than a century’s worth of clean-shaven NYC mayors.

And hey, what better time to revive an early 2010s tradition than following the Democrats’ historic victories in the midterm elections. Millennial woke optimism is back, baby, and so is growing facial hair for a charitable cause. If the mayor’s facial hair can turn a bygone internet fad into renewed attention for men’s health, it may be his most consequential grooming decision yet.

#6660. The Best Nontoxic Cookware Trusted by BA Editors (2026)

If you’ve shopped for nonstick pots and pans in the past decade, you’ve had the term nontoxic cookware thrown at you with increasing velocity. As you've thought about getting new pans you may have even searched for the best nontoxic cookware without being totally sure what “toxins” they supposedly do not have in them. So what exactly makes cookware “toxic,” and why do these “safe” or “healthy” pans claim to be better?

The answer begins with a class of synthetic chemicals known as PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. These chemicals, which repel liquids, have been used in everything from waterproof jackets to nonstick cookware coatings, and after decades of use, the health concerns raised by scientists started to break through to the public more broadly in more recent years.

Whether you’ve never heard of PFAS or you’re already familiar with their nearly 100-year-old history, you’re in the right place if you want to avoid them. We’ve tested dozens of nonstick and “nontoxic” pans to find the best options to help you keep PFAS out of your cookware. Read on for the lowdown on all things nontoxic cookware.

When companies label their cookware “nontoxic,” it’s a marketing move as much as anything, designed to position it as a safer alternative to traditional nonstick, which is typically coated in a chemical called polytetrafluoroethylene, or PTFE. And to understand why people began to colloquially refer to old nonstick pans as “toxic,” we need a little history of PTFE.

Discovered accidentally in 1938 and trademarked by chemical company DuPont as Teflon in the early 1960s, PTFE was an earthquake in the home cookware market during the second half of the 20th century because it provided consumers with a completely nonstick, no-oil-needed cooking surface. By the turn of the century, Teflon had become ubiquitous, finding its way into a staggering number of American kitchens in the form of PTFE-coated skillets, muffin tins, baking dishes, and more.

PTFE, though, is just one of thousands of a class of chemicals in PFAS family mentioned earlier. Around 1951, DuPont started using another PFAS called PFOA (short for perfluorooctanoic acid) in its Teflon manufacturing process. Over time, it became clear that PFOA could enter the human body by way of gaseous fumes or chipped coatings and have detrimental effects on human health and the environment, including increased risk of certain cancers, birth defects, ulcerative colitis, and thyroid disease. Under mounting pressure from public health and environmental advocacy groups, manufacturers phased out PFOA by 2013.

These days traditional nonstick cookware is made using PFOA-free PTFE (which is also typically free of PFOS, another harmful PFAS). You’ll see it marketed under names like T-fal, Dura-Slide, or hard-anodized aluminum. While PTFE itself is considered less harmful than other PFAS, there is still a broader concern. Thousands of PFAS compounds remain unregulated, and there is ongoing research into the class of chemicals as a whole. A label that says “PFOA- and PFOS-free” does not necessarily mean the product is free of all potentially risky chemicals in the PFAS family.

While not necessarily the first recorded use of the term, the idea of “nontoxic” cookware was largely introduced to consumers when GreenPan released the first PFAS-free ceramic nonstick frying pans in 2007. Since then, “nontoxic cookware” has come to mean “PFAS-free nonstick cookware.” While there’s nothing inherently incorrect about this characterization, it’s important to recognize the degree to which it has become a marketing buzzword.

While “nontoxic cookware” typically refers to ceramic nonstick, which is made from silica using a method called the sol-gel process, any cookware that’s made without the use of harmful chemicals like PFAS can be considered “nontoxic.” That includes some tried-and-true options you probably already know and love: stainless steel, cast iron, and carbon steel.

Ceramic nonstick comes closest to mimicking the ease of traditional Teflon, but like any coating, it will degrade over time and can chip (more on that below). That’s why we recommend getting comfortable with uncoated stainless, cast iron, and carbon steel. With the right technique, your food won’t stick to them either, and they’ll last a lot longer.

Available sizes: 8", 10", 12"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: Yes, but hand-washing recommendedMetal-utensil-safe: Theoretically, but wood or silicone recommendedOven-safe: Up to 600ºFWarranty: 1 year

About ceramic nonstick: I have to be honest here, I've personally sworn off coated nonstick pans for good, because no matter which one you buy, it will only last you a few years tops before the coating starts to degrade and you need to replace it. That said, I understand why people gravitate towards them—and if you're dead-set on buying one, ceramic nonstick is the way to go. These pans are typically made of stainless steel or aluminum and lined with a silica-based coating that makes them nice and slick—for a few years, at least. The exact makeup of that coating varies brand to brand, which is why we’ve spent years testing lots of ceramic nonstick pans to find the ones that best deliver on their nonstick promise.

Our top pick: GreenPan’s ceramic nonstick pans were the first to hit the market in 2007, and the brand’s products have consistently come out on top in our best nonstick pan testing. Its Valencia Pro line is our favorite for a few reasons: It’s hefty enough to feel durable while remaining lightweight enough to be easily maneuverable. It’s also affordable enough that you won’t have to break the bank when you inevitably need to replace it in a few years, and more scratch-resistant than some earlier GreenPan iterations we've tried. Oh, and it's induction compatible too.

A budget option: If you don’t cook on an induction stovetop and are looking for a cheaper option, you can go with GreenPan’s Paris Pro line, which performed similarly to the Valencia in our testing.

About carbon nonstick (or nitrided carbon steel): At the outset, these pans act like traditional nonstick but can hold up to high heat, metal utensils, and years of use because they aren’t coated. Instead the carbon steel is nitrided, a process that infuses nitrogen into the metal to make it tougher, slicker, and both corrosion- and rust-resistant.

Our top pick: When we first got a hold of Misen’s Carbon Nonstick pan it seemed like the holy grail for anyone trying to quit Teflon without giving up easy-release eggs. Unlike traditional carbon steel pans, Misen’s version has an aluminum core that heats quickly and evenly, and its surface repels oil straight out of the box. In testing, fried eggs, chicken thighs, and sautéed onions all slid right off with minimal oil (food director Chris Morocco said it was “practically allergic” to eggs). The pan is lightweight and durable and will develop a terrific nonstick seasoning. However, as our lead cookware tester Wilder Davies continued cooking with the Misen, he noticed the initial corn oil seasoning layer started to wear, and the miraculous oil repelling characteristics decreased. Once that happened we assigned four more people, myself included, to work with these pans and we all noticed a reduction in the nonstickiness as time went on. However, the nonstick curve on these has proven to be more U-shaped, as we've continued to cook on and season them, food release started to become easier again.

Available sizes: 10", 12", 14"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 600°FWarranty: Limited lifetime

About stainless steel: Stainless-steel cookware is a staple in home and professional kitchens because of its versatility, durability, and low maintenance needs. Use it on the stovetop, in the oven, or with metal tools—unlike shorter-lived ceramic pans, a stainless-steel skillet can serve you well for a lifetime. And here’s the thing: With the proper technique, stainless steel can release almost as easily as ceramic nonstick. The key in guaranteeing your food slides right off instead of becoming a stuck-on mess is using sufficient fat and heat. Make sure to wait until your oil is shimmering before adding whatever you’re cooking, give it enough time in the pan to let the maillard reaction do its thing, and you should have no issues with stickage.

Our top pick: We’ve tested many types of stainless-steel cookware throughout the years here at BA, and one brand has repeatedly stood out time and time again for its consistently well-made, durable, high-performing products. That brand is All-Clad.

In our testing of stainless-steel frying pans and sauté pans, product testers and Test Kitchen editors alike lauded All-Clad’s D3 Everyday line as the best mix of value and performance for home cooks. The “3” refers to these pans’ 3-ply construction, which features an aluminum core sandwiched between two layers of stainless-steel cladding. That aluminum allows the pan to conduct heat quickly and evenly, and it makes the pan more lightweight than solid stainless-steel cookware. In our testing, we found that those promises held true, and that the D3 pans were easy to clean (just hand-wash with a little soapy water, plus some Bar Keepers Friend if you need a hand getting any remaining bits off) and have continued to perform well over the many years we’ve been using them.

About cast iron: If you’re willing to put just a bit of work into caring for your cookware, a cast-iron skillet will easily fill the nonstick pan-size hole in your kitchen. Cast-iron cookware will never quite reach the level of nonstick that a Teflon-coated piece offers, but in our testing, we’ve found that a properly seasoned cast-iron pan is on par with ceramic nonstick—plus it only gets more slick over time as you continue to use it.

Our top pick: After testing more than 20 cast-iron skillets over several years, our current top pick is the Lancaster No. 8 because it’s lightweight, it has a smooth pre-seasoned surface that’s nice and slick right out of the box, and it provides even heat distribution. The one downside is that it’s quite pricey compared to something like Lodge’s iconic cast iron, which we recommend as a great budget alternative. The Lodge is probably the pan most people think of when they hear “cast-iron skillet,” and at around $20, depending on where and when you buy it, it’s one of the best values in the cookware world—particularly because you can keep it forever rather than replacing it every few years. In our testing, it performed just as well as many more expensive pans.

About enameled cast iron: You may have also heard of enameled cast iron, which is frequently seen in products like our favorite Le Creuset and Staub Dutch ovens. Many people expect enameled cast-iron pots and pans to be nonstick because the ones with light-colored interiors sort of resemble the kinds of ceramic nonstick coatings we wrote about above, but in reality, that’s not the case. That doesn’t mean you can’t cook food in these things without it sticking, but you’ll need to use sufficient fat and heat to make that happen, as you do with a stainless-steel pan. The benefit of enameled cast iron is that it provides superior heat retention and distribution, and protects the cast-iron core from rust and acidity. It's become one of my favorite types of cookware to use at home over the past few years.

Our top pick: The Staub Round Cocotte is my personal top pick when it comes to Dutch ovens, and tied with the Le Creuset in our official product testing. I prefer the Staub’s dark textured enamel interior, which is less prone to showing discoloration. In addition to the round cocotte, I also own the braiser and a deep skillet, both of which I find myself pulling out constantly.

Available sizes: 8", 10.25", 11", 12.5"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 500ºFWarranty: Limited lifetime

About carbon steel: Carbon steel is sort of the Goldilocks cookware because it affords you the nonstick qualities and lightweight feel of a coated nonstick pan and the durability of a cast-iron or stainless-steel skillet. The one caveat is that in order to achieve those nonstick qualities, you’ll need to spend some time properly seasoning your new pan, just as you would with cast iron. But with a bit of work at the outset and occasional maintenance, you’ll be rewarded with an heirloom-worthy piece of cookware that has a well-earned nonstick patina.

Our top pick: De Buyer is one of those famed, old European cookware brands that lots of American home cooks may not be that familiar with. Its “blue” frying pan comes pre-seasoned and will just get better and better as the seasoning improves. As senior writer Wilder Davies notes, you can take specific steps to season it—use a thin layer of oil (as thin as you can possibly get) and put it in a hot oven for an hour—but you can also just keep cooking with it and that seasoning will develop on its own. Another nice feature of this pan in particular, and one that has nothing to do with its seasoning, is its welded-on handle. That means there are no rivets to clean around when you’re done.

Read more about our favorite carbon steel pans.

What types of kitchen gear is PTFE found in?

A skillet may be the first thing you think of when you think of nonstick cookware, but PTFE coatings show up in a host of other items in the kitchen and beyond. On top of skillets, pots, saucepans, and Dutch ovens, you'll also find PTFE in rice cookers, waffle irons, baking sheets, and grill baskets.

You may recognize ceramic nonstick as the material of choice of many of the aesthetically-pleasing, Instagram-viral cookware companies that started popping up in the late 2010s (I’m looking at you, Our Place and Caraway). Ceramic nonstick pans are made without any PFAS. Instead, a gel made from silica is applied and then dried onto the cookware’s metal body to create a nonstick surface.

Sounds great, right? Well, there are a few caveats, the main one being that ceramic nonstick coatings are not built to last. That means you’ll want to be sure to avoid using metal utensils when cooking with them, opting instead for wood or silicone. You’ll also want to avoid exposing them to extremely high temperatures: Even though ceramic cookware is technically more heat tolerant than cookware made with PTFE, high heat will wear down the pan’s ceramic coating. Many manufacturers claim their pans are oven-safe up to certain (often high) temperatures, but we’d recommend using one of our other recommendations above for any stove-to-oven cooking, as those trips to the oven will only further degrade that ceramic coating over time. Similarly, despite any of being dishwasher-safe, hand-washing your pans will prolong their lifespans.

Even if you treat your ceramic nonstick cookware with the utmost care and attention, you still shouldn’t expect it to last you more than one to three years before it starts to lose its nonstick properties. That’s why the best nontoxic nonstick cookware is not necessarily a coated piece of PFOA- or PFAS-free gear—in fact, we’d argue the best nontoxic “nonstick” pans money can buy are made of cast iron, or carbon steel. While these materials are not actually manufactured or marketed as nonstick, each has nonstick properties that can be achieved with proper use and care. .

The bottom line here is that no one needs a coated pan in their life. There is no recipe on this website (or in this world) that requires you to use one, and we tend to think you’re better off investing some time in learning to cook with a more durable type of cookware than spending you money on a full nonstick cookware set. That said, we’re recommending a range of cookware options here for those who are looking for alternatives to traditional PTFE-base nonstick, including a ceramic option for people who aren’t quite ready to kiss coated nonstick goodbye.

#6657. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6656. With Grand Theft Auto VI, Rockstar Bet $1.5B That Humans Could Make a Better Game Than AI

Somewhere in the far north of Leonida, Grand Theft Auto VI’s fictional take on Florida, a robbery is taking place. This much is unsurprising. Crime is baked into the title of the series, which began in 1997 and, despite its thick American accent, is still predominantly made in Scotland. But Jason and Lucia, the young, beautiful Bonnie and Clyde who together share the role of protagonists in GTA VI, are not the ones committing this crime. Rather, a grizzled biker hangs from the second-floor window of a locked bar, throwing valuables down to his accomplice on the street.

A thunderstorm has recently rolled through this area and the tarmac steams as sunlight knifes through the clouds. It’s Leonida-muggy. Patches of sweat swell beneath Jason’s arms as he takes in the scene. The bikers notice you watching and ask, politely, considering the circumstances, if you could fuck off. A choice presents itself: clamber back on your stolen motorbike and continue your road trip, or insert yourself into this micro-drama and take a principled stand on behalf of concerned citizens everywhere (then take the loot for yourself, of course).

Dozens of impromptu moments like this stud GTA6, a video game that makes you feel like one entity among many rather than the spoiled V.I.P. around whom everything has been artfully arranged. Most video games flatter the player by making them the centre of the virtual universe, the cog on which all the digital clockwork turns. What is extraordinary about Vice City and its surrounding area is how much of the world appears to trundle on without needing your presence or input.

These moments are made possible by dozens of interlocking systems built by dozens of discrete teams. An entire Los-Angeles-based team worked on the personalities and behaviors of the thousands of people who inhabit Vice City; the bar’s interior was meticulously set-dressed to suggest the lives and tastes of its proprietors and patrons, while the biker’s dialogue and reactions to your choices were written, cast and performed. The weather, too, is restless: cloud and rain move across the world, dynamically changing light and mood. This tableaux, which only a small percentage of players may ever encounter, has not been staged like a scene in a play but rather cultivated in what amounts to the world’s most expensive Petri dish.

Since 1984, when Elite first used procedural generation to conjure an entire galaxy on a computer screen, game designers have learned to produce universes from scant technological resources. But in the era of procedural generation, scale is almost routine; the harder, more costly work is making an expanse feel handmade and coherent. GTA VI manages both, with districts populated by distinct communities and social strata, each shaped by decades of imagined history. It reveals a kind of detail and thoughtfulness that A.I. has yet to reproduce convincingly—and perhaps never will.

The game’s lavishness is not only visible in the rain, the sweat and the individual strands of hair falling across Lucia’s shoulders, but also in the hundreds, perhaps thousands, of diversions away from the criminal grind. For example, Jason and Lucia can take time out from planning a heist to compete in illegal street races for prize money, enter dirt-bike scrambles or race stock cars in a stadium. You can become a hunter, choosing a rifle to suit your quarry so as not to ruin its pelt; start drone racing, streaking through abandoned buildings in an FPV headset; or dive for treasure among old shipwrecks, dodging both the circling sharks, and the authorities who want to check your license.

A compelling main story runs through the game, with missions that leave room for different approaches: you might play as a careful shooter, aiming to wound rather than kill, or as a less discerning one. The couple, so artfully written and performed, offer vivid points of entry into the world as you guide them from relative poverty towards financial security that, perhaps, might allow them to build a family life beyond crime. But much of the joy comes from straying from the main path.

To that end the game makes room for long, meandering drives across the country and peaceful early-morning flights over mountain ranges. You can spend a sleepy afternoon with a scenic view, peering through dollar-a-minute binoculars. Many of these diversions appeared in the studio’s earlier games, but here they feel newly vivid, rendered with extraordinary fidelity. The smaller encounters are just as memorable. Happen upon a possum at night and it might play dead on the tarmac. In a thrift store, you can while away assembling fits worthy of a Ralph Lauren vintage buyer; at a 24-hour nightclub, you can dance until sunrise, before emerging blinking into the dawn while wondering, as Kanye once put it, if they’ve got cabs still. (Of course they do: you can summon one in an instant from your virtual phone).

This is lavish game-making on an unprecedented scale. The irony, however, is that GTA VI arrives at a moment when other studios are bleeding staff (if they survive at all) and the cost of making games at anywhere close to this level continues to rise precipitously. In one industry survey published this month, a third of respondents said they had been laid off in the past two years; more than half of those laid off had yet to find new work—a stark picture of the ongoing insecurity across the industry. In the early 2010s, game budgets fell between $30 and $70 million. McKinsey puts the current cost of a blockbuster game production at $200 million to $500 million. At these prices, few can pay to play.

Even amid the union-busting allegations (which Rockstar denies; an employment tribunal is ongoing), the company has retained much of its long-serving talent between major releases. That continuity gives it a store of institutional knowledge that is hard to preserve when studios expand and contract around individual projects. Key members of GTA VI’s leadership have worked together for decades. The studio also has a clear commercial advantage over its closest creative peers: Naughty Dog, creator of the Uncharted and The Last of Us series, and CD Projekt Red, creator of The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077. Their story-led games can dominate a moment, but their stories conclude when the credits roll.

After players finished Grand Theft Auto V’s story, by contrast, they could continue to inhabit its world through GTA Online, joining others in an ever-replenishing sandbox of play. A leak of Rockstar data suggested that GTA Online averaged about $9.6 million a week between September 2025 and April 2026—roughly $42 million a month. Rockstar is owned by Take-Two, and there is no evidence that GTA Online’s astonishing revenue was entirely funneled into GTA VI. But a game generating revenue year after year gives its parent a durable source of income, justifying artisanal-style work. These factors make Grand Theft Auto VI’s scale and fidelity exceptionally difficult for any rival to match.

That challenge is something even Rockstar’s former leaders have had to reckon with. Leslie Benzies—who for years was one of the three creative leaders on Rockstar projects alongside Sam and Dan Houser (of the trio, only Sam remains at the company)—founded Build a Rocket Boy, which raised more than $300 million before releasing MindsEye. The game’s troubled launch was followed by mass redundancies and, in September 2026, a slide into administration. The lesson seems clear. Money alone cannot buy the infrastructure, expertise and returning audience that have allowed Rockstar to build this world at extraordinary length.

In a game filled with enticing luxuries, from expensive shoes to glinting supercars, the visible human hand is, in this dawning age of AI abundance, the rarest luxury of all in Leonida. You can leave the bikers to their robbery: clouds drift on, the tarmac dries. The world keeps its own time. Making that unforced life cohere took years of work across many teams, and required a collective attention to every detail. With budgets rising and studios closing, perhaps no other company could afford such a wager. Leonida is a miracle of craft—and a monument to a form of game-making the wider industry can no longer sustain.

#6655. Andrew Scott on Elsinore, the Met Gala, and Why “Shakespeare Is Really for Everybody”

To be or not to be? Andrew Scott knows a thing or two about that question. On Wednesday evening, the Irish actor brought a touch of Shakespearean flair—and plenty of leading-man charisma—to the Museum of Modern Art for the New York premiere of his latest film, Elsinore.

Dressed in a pinstripe suit by Vivienne Westwood, Scott made quite the entrance. Joining him were director Simon Stone, co-star Joe Locke, and members of the film’s creative team, all exchanging warm embraces, big smiles, and the kind of affectionate greetings that made the evening feel less like a formal premiere and more like a particularly well-dressed reunion.

There was plenty to celebrate. Based on a remarkable true story, Elsinore features Scott as Ian Charleson, the Scottish actor best known for his role in Chariots of Fire, during the final months of his life in 1989. As he prepares to take on the titular role of Hamlet at London’s National Theatre, Charleson is privately battling AIDS, though determined to return to the stage despite his deteriorating health. Named after the Danish castle that provides the setting for Shakespeare’s tragedy, the film follows Charleson’s journey toward one final, extraordinary performance, exploring the complicated relationship between art and mortality, and the courage it takes to keep pursuing one’s passion in the face of devastating circumstances.

Also starring Olivia Colman and Luke Thompson, Elsinore finds unexpected lightness in a story shadowed by tragedy. At its heart is a celebration of the transformative power of performance—and of a man whose final act would become one of the most meaningful of his life.

Scott is no stranger to Shakespeare’s most famous prince. His own acclaimed turn as Hamlet in Robert Icke’s 2017 Almeida Theatre production earned him an Olivier Award nomination. His experience with the Bard may make Shakespeare’s lines look effortless, but finding his way into the language is another matter. So what’s his secret? “I always think of it like rap music. If I don’t understand every word when someone is rapping, there’s the energy behind it and the musicality or the velocity of it—and it’s still electrifying,” he told Vogue. “It’s the same with Shakespeare, but I hate the idea that it’s kind of kidnapped by academics. Shakespeare is really for everybody.”

And when it comes to commanding an audience, Scott is something of an expert, though even he admits that some occasions are more nerve-racking than others. Asked whether portraying Hamlet or getting dressed for the Met Gala presents the bigger challenge, he didn’t hesitate. “Playing Hamlet is more intimidating—but only just,” he said with a laugh. “I think with the Met Gala, you always think it’s going to be incredibly intimidating. The stairs are a bit scary, but it’s only clothes! So you’ve just got to have a bit of fun.”

Scott’s greatest challenge in Elsinore was getting beneath the mythology of Charleson and discovering the man himself. What struck him most was the actor’s sense of humor—a quality he was determined to preserve on screen. Despite its emotional weight, Scott insists, this is not a film without comic relief. “It’s a very uplifting and a very funny film,” he said, calling Stephen Beresford’s screenplay “as hysterically funny as it is heartbreaking.”

That humor was also something producer Andrea Occhipinti was keen to protect. His connection to Charleson, however, went far beyond the screen. The two first met in 1984 while working on the television miniseries The Sun Also Rises. As Occhipinti recalled, they became close friends, bonding over the fact that they were the only two gay men in the group. Charleson never disclosed that he was HIV-positive. It was only after his death, when their mutual friend Ethan Silverman shared the story of his final six months, that Occhipinti began to imagine the possibility of a film.

Years later, he found his screenwriter in Beresford and his leading man in Scott. The casting, it seems, was almost written in the stars. Asked what Charleson might have thought of the film and the evening’s celebrations, Occhipinti said he was certain his friend would approve. “Ian would be pleased because Andrew Scott is amazing. He really looks like Ian and he has incredible talent. I think he would have smiled about all of this tonight. He very much was a loving and warm person.”

That celebratory spirit carried into the evening, which brought out a suitably starry crowd. Among those on hand to mark the occasion were Sigourney Weaver, Ben Platt, Dylan Mulvaney, Patricia Clarkson, Katie Couric, François Arnaud of Heated Rivalry, And Just Like That’s Sarita Choudhury, Kate Walsh, and Christopher Meloni.

And no Shakespearean celebration would be complete without a little drama after the curtain fell. The festivities continued at Le Rock, where guests gathered for the after-party, eager to congratulate Scott, exchange a few words, and sing his praises. Over Champagne and conversation, partygoers tucked into sliders and fries, while an impressive seafood display piled high with fresh lobster, oysters, and shrimp provided a lavish centerpiece.

Naturally, Shakespeare had the last word on the evening’s décor, too. Copies of Hamlet were scattered throughout the restaurant, alongside a rather cheeky nod to one of the play’s most memorable scenes. A skull emblazoned with the words “This is what you’ll look like by the end of it”—a joke that also features in the film—added a deliciously irreverent touch. It was a fitting detail for a celebration of a story that finds plenty of laughter amid the tragedy. The party carried on well past midnight, with no one seemingly in a hurry to call it a night.

#6653. What You Need to Know About Japanese Knives

The popularity of Japanese knives in home and commercial kitchens has exploded in the last few years, and for good reason: A lot of them outperform their Western counterparts in kitchen tests. Western-style knives are bulkier, all-purpose kitchen tools—years ago, it would be common for many chefs to use the heavy bolster near the heel of the blade to crack open a can of tomatoes during service. Japanese knives (and Japanese-style knives produced by manufacturers elsewhere) are designed with precision cuts in mind and usually have a specific purpose. However, because they’re designed with that specificity in mind, it can be tricky to know what you need and what you’ll use.

Thankfully, we’ve reviewed a wide variety of Japanese-style knives for Bon Appétit and have assembled a roundup to help you identify exactly what your kitchen needs. While there are more styles of Japanese knives than those listed here, these options have all been thoroughly tested, giving us the confidence to speak to each knife’s utility. Before we jump into specific styles, however, it’s useful to give a quick rundown on some of the broad strokes of what makes a Japanese-style knife unique.

Many Japanese knives are designed for push cuts or pull-through slicing rather than the rocking chop of a heavy Western chef’s knife. They tend to have a straighter edge than their Western counterparts, making them slightly less adept at speeding through a mince of herbs, but more precise in their cuts. Most Japanese-style knives also feature a sheep’s-foot tip that curves down to the point, giving the user more control over fine-point work.

Japanese knives are often made with a harder steel than their Western counterparts. Harder steel helps a knife’s edge retain sharpness, which lets manufacturers use steeper sharpening angles for a finer edge. This helps most Japanese knives slice more delicately than Western knives, though harder steel can chip on material like ice or bone.

Traditional Japanese-style knives are only sharpened on one side, giving them a much finer edge than the 50/50 bevel of Western-style knives that are sharpened on both sides. Some modern Japanese knife makers have pivoted to a 50/50 style bevel for ease of sharpening; however, when you’re shopping, you’ll encounter plenty of knives with 70/30 bevel with the inside edge (the left edge for a right-handed knife) sharpened at a steeper angle. A 70/30 bevel is easier to maintain than a single-bevel but offers a sharper edge than a 50/50 bevel.

Many traditional Japanese kitchen knives feature a wa-style handle—an octagonal wood handle that envelops a hidden knife tang (the metal part of the knife that connects to the handle). Wa-style handles help keep knives lighter and nimbler, while many Western-style knives use full-tang construction, adding weight and heft to the blade. Many modern Japanese knife makers, though, combine full-tang knife handles with Japanese blade shapes to create a hybrid-style knife that’s both durable and adept at slicing.

The gyuto, or Japanese chef’s knife, originated in Japan in the early 1900s, when French cooking began to gain popularity in a rapidly modernizing country. This knife style took cues from the traditional French chef’s knife and combined them with elements of traditional Japanese knife making. The resulting Japanese take on a chef’s knife was primarily designed for slicing meat, though it also features a curved edge that makes it easy to chop herbs. Compared to a Western chef’s knife, the gyuto has a straighter blade and a drop point tip with a lower overall profile. This is primarily designed so that the user can place the knife’s tip on the cutting board and draw it through food, taking advantage of the gyuto’s sharp edge and thin blade for precision slicing. But while the gyuto excels at slicing meat, its general shape makes it an overall great pick to anchor your knife collection, and many home cooks opt for a gyuto as their daily driver over a traditional chef’s knife.

We’ve long been fans of the gyuto fan here at Bon Appétit, with MAC’s Professional Hollow Ground Chef’s Knife topping our chef’s knife review for years. For a wicked sharp, more traditional option, we really like the Kazan Arare by Shibata gyuto, which impressed us so much we had to give it its own review.

Increasingly common as a part of brands’ knife sets, the santoku knife is a relatively modern knife shape, first appearing in the 1940s or so. Nicknamed the three virtues knife, the santoku draws on the gyuto, nakiri, and deba to create a well-rounded utility knife that’s great for cutting meat, fish, and vegetables. Typically, these knives feature a pretty steep sheep’s-foot tip for precision point work, a tall heel for push cuts, and just enough curve for pull-through slicing and rock-chopping. A santoku knife is great for well-rounded utility work—think cutting cheese and an apple for a snack, slicing leftover roasted chicken to make a sandwich, or dicing an onion for a curry.

Typically, we like a santoku knife that’s between six and seven inches, so it contrasts with the longer gyuto. Our favorite overall model is the MAC Professional Santoku Knife, but if you’d like a razor-sharp version with a traditional wa-style handle, we love the Kazan Ginsan Nashiji Santoku.

Nakiri knives have a straight edge and a sturdy spine, specifically designed for chopping vegetables. Sometimes referred to as a vegetable cleaver, the nakiri excels at push cuts, making it great for both matchsticking carrots and breaking down tough-skinned squash. Since most gyutos feature thin blades and fine edges, the nakiri also holds a spot in the Japanese knife lineup as a tougher, heavier knife for more demanding tasks. Traditional nakiri knives may also feature a blunt, rounded tip, which can be rotated against the cutting board to create a smooth, chopping motion.

The Tojiro DP Damascus Nakiri is by far our overall favorite tested nakiri knife for its extremely sharp edge and overall balance, but it’s also pricey. We also really like the Tojiro Classic nakiri, though it can have stock issues due to its popularity and price point.

The deba knife is a traditional Japanese knife designed for fish butchery. Unlike a Western fillet knife, which is designed to be flexible and nimble, the deba is a heavy, sturdy blade with a thick spine that gives the heel of the blade a cleaver-like feel. But a deba knife is also designed for precision slicing, and it usually features a traditional single-bevel edge. That single-bevel edge allows the knife to come to a finer point than a double-bevel edge, and the sheep’s-foot tip adds to the deba knife’s ability to portion out delicate fish fillets as well.

We haven’t tested deba knives because they require a bit of knowledge and skill to use them for breaking down whole fish, but if you’re intrigued by the shape and want a cleaver-like knife for your kitchen, the Seki Mago Roku Deba from Kai is an affordable, solid option. Otherwise, we think most people would be better served looking to a nakiri or santoku knife.

Named for the French word petite, which means small, the petty knife is often a replica of the gyuto, just in a much, much smaller form. Most petty knives are around five inches long and feature a thin, lightly curved blade with a drop point tip and heel just tall enough to keep your fingers from bashing into the cutting board. Petty knives are great utility knives for small tasks, like dicing a shallot, slicing garlic, or slicing herbs, but they’re also long and nimble enough to be great slicers. Unless you do a lot of handheld turning and peeling, a petty knife is a great replacement for a paring knife in your lineup.

We found that both the MAC Professional Petty Knife and the Tojiro Classic Petty Knife were sharp enough to slice a steak while still being the perfect size to slice strawberries for your morning yogurt bowl.

Traditionally a fisherman’s knife used for all sorts of purposes on the boat, the funayuki is an old-school knife shape that predates the gyuto and santoku, and it likely helped inspire both shapes. The traditional funayuki is a shorter knife, around seven inches long, with a narrow, pointed tip and a tall heel. They are santoku-sized but gyuto-shaped. Unlike the deba knife, which was a heavy, single-bevel knife used for fish butchery, the funayuki was designed to be light and nimble so that fishermen could fillet their lunch while at sea. These days, most home cooks might pick up a funayuki as a secondary, shorter gyuto, or opt for this shape over a santoku as an all-purpose utility knife with a narrower tip.

Though it’s not as common in modern kitchens, one of our favorite Japanese chef’s knives is the Akiru-Saku Funayuki Gyuto, which is more traditionally shaped like a funayuki but is advertised as a gyuto since the two shapes are so similar.

The kiritsuke is a Japanese slicing knife with an angular “sword tip” that allows the user to make precision cuts. The initial design combined a long slicing shape and tall heel, making the kiritsuke a hybrid knife, similar to the santoku. For most people, the kiritsuke will be a version of an all-purpose chef’s knife that could take the place of a gyuto as a daily driver, with the big difference coming in the shape of the tip.

When reviewing chef’s knives, we found that the Shun Classic Kiritsuke was a great all-purpose chef’s knife with a unique tip that some people might prefer over a gyuto, since it curves upward more like a Western chef’s knife and allows for more of a rock chop motion.

Boning and fillet knives are often unitaskers that don’t see much use unless you’re a fan of home butchery, but the Japanese honesuki is an even more specialized boning knife shape. Designed specifically for poultry, the honesuki is a steep, wedge-shaped knife with a very fine point and a tall heel. The goal is to have a knife that’s delicate enough to slip between a chicken joint while being sturdy enough to cut through cartilage. While the honesuki was designed for a specific purpose, we find that this shape is more versatile and can be swapped in for a petty knife for other small chopping and dicing tasks in ways that a curved fillet knife can’t.

We like the MAC Professional Honesuki as a great option that could tackle most boning-knife tasks while remaining sharp and versatile enough for utility work. If you find yourself breaking down a whole chicken while also wanting a strawberry-slicing knife, the honesuki could be a nonconventional multitasker.

#6652. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6651. 15 Best Beard Oils for Taming Your Stubborn Facial Hair

So, you've realized. Growing a beard was only the beginning: Now you’ve gotta give it some love. Thankfully, the best beard oil will keep that sculpted scruff feeling great! And not just for you, either, because the right beard oil leaves your skin glowing—and stops your facial hair from annoying any partner who gets close to it. Great beard oils also keep coarse hair from getting brittle and wiry, and soften your beard so you’re not scratching your neck or dealing with beard dandruff (yes, it exists). All that from just a couple drops of wonder oil.

I’d go so far as to rank beard oil as the second most important beard care product, just after beard trimmers. And it’s a close second. Because whether you keep your facial hair at a precise 24-hour stubble, go full hermit-mode, or stay somewhere in between, a beard oil does irreplaceable work. (The kind you can’t replace with any old moisturizer or conditioner.) So, if you’re tired of flyaways, coarse beard hair, dandruff, or itchiness, these GQ-tested and approved beard oils will turn your scruff into fluff. Promise.

For the longest time, I thought of Honest Amish as “that Amazon beard oil,” given its enormous popularity on the e-tailer. (At the time of writing, we’re talking nearly 30,000 reviews and a 4.5-star rating.) And often, I'll intentionally seek out an alternative to these Amazon-beloved grooming products—if only because it feels like the equivalent of recommending Applebee's to an out-of-towner. But this time, well: Welcome to Applebee's.

Frankly, I couldn't find a better beard oil. Not only is Honest Amish cost-effective (at the second-best price-per-ounce on my list), but the brand nailed the blend. It's a pure oil recipe (no non-oil ingredients), with seven carrier oils and seven essential oils that give it an earthy scent and help tone the skin beneath your bushel. It absorbs fast, works great to smooth down flyaways, relax stiff bristles, and battle both dry skin and flake-prone beards. And did I mention the value? Six bucks per ounce is a steal.

To be clear, I only use Honest Amish on my beard, largely because I'm not a fan of using any essential oils on bare skin—I particularly find that pumpkin seed oil (a key ingredient here) can be slightly pore-clogging on acne-prone skin. That said: I count myself as acne-prone and haven't had issues with Honest Amish, so I'm probably being over-cautious. It's really just that good.

Despite the name Beardbrand, this company's product line covers the whole body, with a focus on multi-tasking grooming products like dual washes, all-purpose balms, and this utilitarian oil. You'll catch me using it on my hands, elbows, and hair—whether for a dash of shine (to offset a matte hair product) or a protective coat against frizz and humidity. But Beardbrand's Utility Oil is on this list because it works beautifully in the beard.

Sure, it's a touch heavier than some other oils—but that also makes it a terrific pre-shave lubricant. It's important to note that no matter which “flavor” you choose, this oil has a strong dash of fragrance. They're all good, but I'm partial to the brand's new Bold Fortune scent, which oozes a sexy combo of leather, oud, and tobacco. (And pro-tip: The brand's utility wash has the same come-hither scent, if you want to double down.)

Horace's beard oil will make a lot of you happy, though for different reasons. For those overwhelmed by scents—particularly artificial ones—you'll appreciate that its got the subtlest of aromas. I'm partial to the Lemon & Mint one, which reads as “fresh" and never overwhelms. For those looking to stay away from chemicals, Horace's formula is 99% natural—and the 1% is a synthetic grapeseed oil, not something with 12 syllables, which I'm fine with.

The brand gets bonus marks for its easily-understood ingredients labels, which break down these details and err on the side of much-appreciated transparency. Finally, if you're on the fence about beard oils, Horace will make you a believer. It absorbs fast, gives a pinch of shine, and makes just enough difference in terms of taming, moisturizing, and softening that you'll see why a beard oil makes sense.

In the grooming world, Jack Black (the brand) has earned its own fanbase, thanks in large part to one product—the signature Jack Black beard oil. Apply just a few drops and it immediately goes to work softening coarse and brittle facial hair, and without an overpowering fragrance that will distract you all day long. It's one of the most popular beard oils on Amazon, but don't hold that against it. While it softens and adds shine, this oil also delivers a dose of antioxidants and vitamins from natural ingredients such as brown algae and rosemary.

It also uses a unique blend of oils with the subtlest whiff of melon fragrance. Instead of the usual suspects (jojoba, avocado, sunflower seed), this product uses Kalahari melon oil, marula oil, and plum oil, which moisturize your facial hair and skin on contact. Because these oils are all fast-absorbing (my beard hair soaks it up like a sponge), they make this product much less greasy than other beard oils, giving it a more premium feel.

I test literally hundreds of grooming products a year, and I'm so intimately acquainted with brands new and old that I often think about them based on their best product. For Pura d'Or, it's this organic beard oil. It's the best value on this list, at $3 per fluid ounce. Given how quickly you can go through beard oil—just think, if you're applying up to twice a day, that dollar-per-ounce math becomes important. So, in addition to being my budget pick, this also gets my recommendation as the best beard oil for big beards.

Of course, it's only important if the formula measures up—and here, it does. There are two carrier oils, argan and jojoba, along with a bit of grapefruit peel and some sandalwood essential oil for both a natural scent and a touch of antimicrobial powers. It's a great beard oil for anyone, no matter how big your bank account, but if you're bearding on a budget, you'll appreciate how much goodness Pura d'Or packs into a few bucks.

Blind Barber's tonka-tinged oil is wonderful for the guy who wants to moisturize skin and whiskers with the same product. It wears extremely light—so much so that my oily skin barely registers its presence—and I find its carrier-oil-centric and shea-butter-forward formula especially comforting on the skin. It should be noted that this formula includes artificial perfume, so fragrance-averse individuals should steer clear. But for those of us who want a special scent, a flake-free beard, and soothed skin, Blind Barber's beard oil does it all.

While I'd use most of the above options as both a hair oil and a beard oil, Aesop's is one where I think of it as a hair oil first and foremost. It brings control without making things look greasy, while trapping moisture and stopping frizz. I'll use it in short hair to tame down the sides, in medium lengths (mixed with a cream or clay) for added shine, or in long hair to prevent split ends. Then, once my hair's settled up, I'll run my hands through my beard afterward. So, if you want a great hair oil with beard benefits, Aesop's is the winner.

Since the beginning of the men's grooming boom, I've been waiting for the big designer fashion houses to start catering to guys with facial hair. For now, Tom Ford's beard oil stands alone. So, how does the designer oil stack up against our everyday favorites? After trying it out, I can tell you it’s better as a fragrance than a beard oil, but the scent alone earns it a spot in this guide.

The tobacco vanilla fragrance is much more sophisticated than what we’re used to seeing, or smelling, in this space. The scent puts an emphasis on vanilla, and you just need one or two pumps for full coverage. Considering the price and the name on the bottle, we were shocked to find this oil comes in a plastic pump bottle, but that fragrance. If you want to buy beard oil as a gift, this premium conditioning oil is a step up over your average Amazon brand, even if it doesn't soften coarse hair as well as some of our other options.

If you have sensitive skin—or if you're afraid of your beard oil clashing with your daily cologne—then Marlowe makes one of the only fragrance-free beard oils. Most beard oil formulas contain both essential oils and some type of perfume oil (or, parfum, for my fellow ingredients detectives), which can be risky for your skin, follicles, and pores, so it’s nice to have an option for acne-prone and sensitive skin types.

This beard oil couldn’t be simpler—and I mean that in a good way. Marlowe No. 143 has an all-oil formula and just four ingredients: safflower seed oil, sunflower seed oil, corn oil, and soybean oil. That’s it. Considering the average beauty product contains up to a dozen ingredients we can’t even pronounce, it’s a refreshing change. Although, I have to say, if you want the softest possible beard, Honest Amish also makes a fragrance-free oil.

Most guys use beard oil to tame flyaways. But what if you want the thickest, fullest beard possible? In that case, I’d recommend reaching for Bevel’s oil. This brand makes skin and hair products for Black men, but anyone with coarse or curly hair can benefit from their products. GQ contributor Timothy Beck Werth reports that this oil gave him a thicker-looking beard without excess frizz, which isn't easy to do. (BTW, that’s as much as you can expect from any beard oil, so please don’t fall for the “beard growth serums” you’ll find all over the internet.)

For parched facial hair, the grapeseed, macadamia, jojoba, and argan oil will condition your beard and add a healthy shine. For beneath the scruff, the avocado and primrose oil with soothe your skin without clogging up your pores and follicles. Werth says this beard oil instantly softened his facial hair, and he also liked the sweeter smell of the macadamia-based formula. Most beard oils opt for woodsy fragrances, and the more subtle scent profile here is a nice surprise, he explains.

Anthony’s conditioning beard oil is a 2-in-1 product—a pre-shave oil and regular beard oil. That approach can be risky, since a lot of multipurpose products try to be everything and succeed at nothing, but luckily that’s not the case here. If you regularly cycle between clean-shaven, stubble, and full-on lighthouse keeper, then you can still use this product daily. As a pre-shave oil, it moisturizes the skin and softens facial hair for a smoother shave with fewer morning-after red bumps. As a beard oil, it hydrates, then locks in that moisture so your beard stays soft and shiny all day. I found the consistency to be somewhere in between a leave-in conditioner gel and a traditional oil, making it thicker and less messy to apply.

The oil also has an herbaceous, minty fragrance that’s so refreshing it feels like aromatherapy every time you run it through your hair. That’s because the formula is full of ingredients that smell good, feel good, and actually help your skin and hair. It uses carrier oils like soybean and castor to deliver skin-pleasing and antimicrobial botanicals such as rosemary, basil, tea tree oil, eucalyptus, and spearmint. And on the hydration front, calendula and olive oil nourish your whiskers into their softest, fluffiest selves. Because of the more complex fragrance and ingredients profile, this wouldn’t be my pick for guys with sensitive skin. Still, it’s a multi-functional serum you’ll look forward to using every day.

Lots of beard oils promise to get flyaways under control, yet those rogue hairs keep popping up. So, what do you do? Instead of trying yet another oil, try reaching for a product that’s more of a leave-in conditioner for your beard. We’ve previously praised Zeus’s beard brushes, but the California-based brand also makes a beard serum that deserves a spot in your bathroom cabinet. I love that this beard oil has the simplest possible ingredients list: sweet almond oil, soybean oil, argan seed oil, trihydroxystearin, avocado oil, and fragrance.

The only multi-syllable ingredient there is a simple thickening agent, which gives this refined beard oil a gel-like consistency. That thicker formula will also put flyaways in their place. The very subtle fragrance is more Mediterranean than winter pine forest (we tested the Verbena Lime version), but you can also opt for a fragrance-free formula if you have sensitive skin or allergies. The plastic bottle uses an air pump, letting you get every last drop of oil. For clean freaks who hate the messiness and spillage that always comes with beard oil application, this is another bonus.

Tired of being left out of couple’s skincare night just because those stupid sheet masks won’t hold onto your glorious beard? Cardon’s got you, boo. Actually, this bead oil hack is perfect for guys who only sparingly use beard oil on an as-needed basis.

The bamboo and charcoal sheet mask is specially shaped for guys with beards, and each mask comes with a dose of beard oil made with argan and jojoba oil. In the Venn diagram of Korean skincare and beard care products, this sheet mask-beard oil duo is the tiny, microscopic bit of overlap in the middle.

The best best oil should support your skin and your beard, and Baxter of California's sweet-smelling oil doesn't sacrifice one for the other. In his guide to the best beard care products, GQ's Timothy Beck Werth said that “In our testing, no beard oil absorbs as quickly or spreads as evenly as this one.” Squalane helps nourish the most overlooked skin on your face, while avocado oil, vitamin E, and botanical extracts smooth out your beard.

As with anything you put on your skin, the ingredients are what matter most. And with beard oils, there are two categories of ingredients: carrier oils and essential oils. No two ingredients will perform exactly the same. Some will help with very specific situations or conditions; some may actively aggravate your skin. Essential oils in particular can aggravate skin if used by themselves. So, consider the following carrier oils and essential oils, favored both by myself and Alyssa Bachowski, a senior barber at Fellow Barber’s Williamsburg, NYC barbershop.

Carrier oils—often vegetable and see oils—make up the bulk of these beard oil formulas, bringing beard nourishment and skin hydration. The most popular carrier oils are argan oil and jojoba oil (both of which Bachowski recommends), though there are dozens of varieties, from castor to marula to grape seed oils. They're usually unscented, though some—like coconut oil—may carry an aroma. Because carrier oils make up the “base” of the oil, they should be among the first to appear in a product's formula or list of ingredients.

“Jojoba oil is non-comedogenic, which means it will not clog your pores. It is also a lighter oil that is absorbent, so it won't just sit on top of the hair and give you a greasy appearance,” Bachowski notes. Along with argan oil, you’re going to see a lot of jojoba oil in most popular beard oil blends.

“Argan oil is filled with a ton of vitamins and minerals, as well as linoleic acid, sterolins, and squalene. All of these aid in protecting and keeping your skin and beard healthy,” Bachowski says.

“Castor oil is known for promoting beard hair growth,” says Bachowski. It’s hypothetically the best beard-growth oil of the crew, because it acts like a vitamin for your strands—though there's more on that below in the FAQs. But don't expect it to grow more hairs, or thicker hairs. Castor oil does have a smoke-and-mirrors benefit, at least. “It is a heavier oil and dark in color, so it can give the appearance of a denser beard on men with dark facial hair,” Bachowski says.

Grape seed oil can help tone down your skin's oil production, and is extremely moisturizing for scruff and skin alike.

Rich in fatty acids, this is a frontrunner for “most nourishing oil” for your skin and whiskers.

Yes, shea butter is in fact a carrier oil, and it has supremely moisturizing properties that make it great for detangling scraggly beards and softening stiff hairs.

Essential oils are distillations from more potent sources, and they tend to be additive—and active—ingredients in a beard oil. These oils are typically extracted through steaming methods, and their range of benefits can include antimicrobial properties, oil-toning abilities, and soothing superpowers. Typically, any natural fragrance in a beard oil will come from essential oils. But pure essential oils can be extremely damaging to the skin.

“You should not apply pure essential oil to a beard—it will do the opposite of what you are trying to achieve,” Bachowski says. “These [pure oils] are not good for your beard nor your skin. as they can be irritating and harmful. Essential oils can cause dryness, itchiness, and redness—and some people may have allergic reactions to them.” This is exactly why you want beard oils from trusted, tested brand.

Bachowski likes cedarwood oil for its naturally astringent properties. “It helps cleanse the pores and prevent ingrown hairs,” she adds. It also adds a natural fragrance.

“Sandalwood has anti-inflammatory properties that help reduce any skin irritation,” Bachowski says of this deliciously scented oil.

Lavender helps calm inflammation and redness, says Bachowski. Plus it brings lavender's soothing scent.

This antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, oil-toning ingredient is terrific for acne-prone faces and oily skin types.

Along with its refreshing scent, grapefruit peel oil helps nourish and detangle.

As GQ's lead grooming product reviewer, I've tried just about every beard oil in the biz. The ones chosen for this roundup excel at protecting and moisturizing both skin and hair, with minimal risk for things like inverse reactions and blemishes. They absorb cleanly, unless they expressly choose not to (like those which expressly use silicone), and they smell terrific (with both natural and artificially scented options). I've tested beard oils for a decade, on a beard that's been long, short, and everything in between. I've also scoured online reviews to confirm that these products are backed by throngs of loyal fans, whose collective opinion echoes my own experiences.

What is the best beard oil according to GQ?

With more than a decade of testing beard oils under his belt, GQ’s expert tester chose Honest Amish as the best beard oil. And 29,000 Amazon shoppers have rated this same product 4.5 out of 5 stars.

What is the difference between beard balm vs. oil?

Both beard balm and beard oil are both terrific for facial hair—but they don't do the same job. Beard balm is optimal for taming and styling facial hair, especially at medium and longer lengths. Beard oil provides less control over the shape and style, but is excellent at softening and conditioning the hairs and the skin underneath (preventing beard itch, beard dandruff, and split ends).

After using a beard wash, most beard oils are applied the same way: “Start off with 2-3 drops in the palm of your hand,” says Bachowski. “Rub it into your hands so that it is evenly distributed from fingertips to the heel of your hand. Start by rubbing the oil with your fingertips onto the skin beneath the beard hair, then eventually working the oil from root to tip of the actual beard. Make sure to also apply oil to your neck and cheeks where you may have shaved or trimmed as well. If you feel like the 2-3 drops wasn't enough based on the length or density of your beard, apply another 2-3 drops.”

Preventing beard dandruff starts with changing your skincare regimen. Namely, introducing exfoliation and moisturizing products that can get past a thick nest of facial hair. For exfoliation, look for physical scrubs (even a beard brush will work). For the best moisturizing effects, be sure to apply beard oil both morning and night. The beard oil will also soften and condition the facial hair to prevent itchiness.

No, beard oil is not meant to help beard hair growth, whether that’s to make facial hair thicker or grow faster. To be honest, we don’t know of much that can really change your scruff's density besides a beard transplant and maybe minoxidil. Beard oil is here to make your existing beard hair softer and more cooperative, while also nourishing the skin beneath the beard—skin that’s often prone to dehydration and dandruff. It’s already doing a lot.

Absolutely. Beard oil is a great investment for anyone with facial hair, since it can help soften and tame your scruff while simultaneously moisturizing the skin underneath. This means no more itching, no flyaways, and no beard dandruff.

Alyssa Bachowski is a senior barber at Fellow Barber’s Williamsburg NYC barbershop location.

#6650. Best Corn Casserole

In my opinion, corn casserole is the most underrated Thanksgiving side. Don’t get me wrong, I love classic stuffing and mashed potatoes, but for me, this is the dish that the holiday isn’t complete without. This tried-and-true recipe is my go-to; it's packed with sweet corn, balanced by a pinch of paprika and herby chives, and has an insanely tender and custardy texture that will have you on your third helping before you even know what hit you. Let this classic side be the star of your Thanksgiving dinner if you’re ever in the mood for endless praise and compliments.

What People Are Saying:“Very delicious, made it exactly like written, came out perfectly.” - mgnpanossia4246

After greasing your baking dish (very well) with softened butter and preheating the oven, break out that box of Jiffy mix. Whisk the mix with granulated sugar in a bowl until very few lumps remain.

Then mix—in a medium bowl or large measuring cup—your eggs, milk, cream, and melted butter until combined. Add that bowl into your Jiffy mix bowl, and stir until just combined. You don’t have to overmix here. Stir in your (thawed!) corn, creamed corn, salt, paprika, and pepper.

Pour your mixture into your prepared baking dish, using a spatula to smooth out the top. Bake until the casserole has fully set and the top is golden brown. This should take anywhere from 40 to 50 minutes.

Once done, let it cool slightly before serving, and top with fresh chives.

The full ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Since only 10 minutes of prep go into this corn casserole, you’ll have plenty of time to pull together the rest of dinner as it bakes in the oven. Try this with simple air-fryer chicken thighs or a hearty harvest chicken skillet for a comforting weeknight dinner, or add it to your holiday sides of mashed potato casserole, sweet potato casserole, and butternut squash mac & cheese alongside your roast turkey.

If you want to make your holiday easier, then this corn casserole is a perfect make-ahead Thanksgiving recipe. Simply prepare the casserole, then cover it tightly and store it in the fridge for up to 48 hours. Remove and bake once you're ready to serve, keeping in mind that it may take slightly longer to bake coming straight from the fridge.

If you somehow manage to have any leftovers, tightly cover your casserole dish or store it in an airtight container in the fridge for 4-5 days.
